intro: Three entries, and one of them is why anyone drives out to Johns Island. The Angel Oak is a live oak wide enough to shade a quarter of an acre, standing in a free city park twenty five minutes from downtown, and the age printed on the souvenirs is roughly four times the age in the records. Out at Middleton Place stands another live oak claimed even older, though its number is legend rather than measurement. In town, the fenced yard of oaks around an 1857 cistern at the College of Charleston completes the list.
meta_description: Charleston's Angel Oak shades a quarter of an acre in a free city park on Johns Island. Where it stands, and how old it actually is.
question_meta: Charleston's oldest tree is the Angel Oak on Johns Island, put at 300 to 500 years. Where it stands, and why 1,500 is the wrong number.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Charleston is the Angel Oak, a southern live oak standing in a free city-owned park at 3688 Angel Oak Road on Johns Island, about twenty five minutes by car from downtown. The City of Charleston, which has owned the park since 1991, puts it at 300 to 400 years; an academic estimate cited by Wikipedia runs to 500. This page carries the union of the two, 300 to 500 years. The 1,500 year figure that appears on signs, postcards and merchandise around the city has no measurement behind it. A third tree, the Middleton Oak at Middleton Place, is sometimes quoted at 900 to 1,000 years, a figure repeated from account to account rather than measured; treat it the same way as the debunked 1,500-year claim for the Angel Oak, a number nobody has actually derived.
question_context: Nobody has counted the rings of the Angel Oak and nobody is going to. Live oak grows fast when young, slows at no reliable rate afterwards and hollows out from the centre while the tree is still healthy, so there is no continuous core to pull and no ring sequence to read. Every published age for it is an estimate built from size, which is how the city arrives at 300 to 400 years and an academic estimate reaches 500. The popular claim that goes with the 1,500 year figure, that this is the oldest living thing east of the Mississippi, does not survive checking either: bald cypress in the Carolinas have been dated by ring count well past a thousand years, one of them beyond 1,600. What is firm is everything that was actually measured. The trunk is 25 and a half feet round by the city's figure and 28 feet by another, the crown shades about 17,000 square feet, and the longest limb reaches 187 feet. The Cistern Yard stand downtown carries no age, because part of it was replanted after Hurricane Hugo.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Charleston?
faq.a: The Angel Oak on Johns Island, put at 300 to 400 years by the City of Charleston and up to 500 by an academic estimate. Nobody has cored it, and live oak cannot be dated by ring count once it hollows, so the range is the honest answer.

faq.q: Is the Angel Oak really 1,500 years old?
faq.a: No. That number circulates locally and on merchandise, and no measurement supports it. Every estimate that starts from the tree itself lands between 300 and 500 years.

faq.q: Is the Angel Oak free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It is a city park, open Monday to Saturday 9am to 5pm and Sunday 1pm to 5pm, closed on holidays. Donations are welcomed. Blankets, food, drinks, props and tripods are not allowed near the tree, which is worth knowing before you arrive with a camera bag.

faq.q: Can I walk into the Cistern Yard at the College of Charleston?
faq.a: Yes, it is an open campus green and self-guided visits are welcome in daylight. It is occasionally roped off for commencement or for Spoleto Festival performances staged in the yard.

faq.q: Isn't the Middleton Oak older than the Angel Oak?
faq.a: Middleton Place quotes 900 to 1,000 years for its oak, but that figure is repeated from one write-up to the next rather than measured, much like the discredited 1,500-year claim once made for the Angel Oak. The Angel Oak's 300 to 500 year range comes from an actual size-based estimate, which is why it keeps the title here.

trees.name: The Angel Oak

location.address: 3688 Angel Oak Road, Johns Island, Charleston, SC 29402

trees.story:
The souvenirs say 1,500 years. The city that owns the tree says 300 to 400, and an academic estimate stretches it to 500. That gap is not carelessness, it is live oak. The species grows fast when young, slows unpredictably and rots out from the middle while the crown is still healthy, so there is no core to pull and nothing to count. What can be measured is girth, and every estimate that starts from the tree itself lands in the hundreds of years rather than the thousands.

None of the size is in dispute. The trunk runs 25 and a half feet round by the city's figure, 28 by another. The crown shades around 17,000 square feet, a quarter of an acre under one tree, and the longest limb travels 187 feet before it stops. Live oak does not race upward; it spreads until the branches come back down and rest on the ground, which is why most of this tree is at eye level.

The name is prosaic. Justus Angel and Martha Waight Tucker Angel owned the estate, and the tree took their surname. The local stories about the spirits of enslaved people appearing among the branches came afterwards.

Hurricane Hugo went over it in 1989 and it recovered. The city bought the land in 1991 and now runs it as a free park taking around 400,000 visitors a year.
trees.access: Free, city-owned park, open 7 days a week (Mon-Sat 9am-5pm, Sun 1pm-5pm), closed holidays. No blankets, drinks, food, props or tripods allowed near the tree; donations welcomed.
trees.transport: On Johns Island, roughly 20-25 minutes by car from downtown Charleston; no direct transit, parking on site
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its huge low, spreading crown, shading a quarter acre, whose branches rest on the ground rather than reaching upward, on a trunk about 7.8m round. It stands within its own fenced park on Johns Island.

trees.name: The Cistern Yard Oaks

location.address: 66 George Street, Charleston, SC 29424 (College of Charleston campus)
location.neighbourhood: Downtown Charleston / College of Charleston campus

trees.story:
Nobody has published an age for a single tree in this yard, and the honest reason is that they are not all the same age. Hurricane Hugo came through Charleston in 1989 and took some of these oaks with it, so what stands now is a mix of the survivors and what went in afterwards. It reads as one thing regardless, which is the whole point of the place: a compact, iron-fenced yard of live oaks hung with Spanish moss, closed at the end by the portico of Randolph Hall.

That building went up between 1828 and 1830 and is a National Historic Landmark. The cistern the yard is named for came later, in 1857, a sunken brick reservoir that once held the campus water supply and now works as the low stage everyone ends up sitting on. Before the College took the ground over in 1785 it was a colonial military barracks.

It is still a working space rather than a lawn to look at. Commencement happens here, and the Spoleto Festival puts performances under the trees, so it is occasionally roped off.

Come in from George Street and stand at the cistern. If anyone has ever dated the older oaks, the College's own records would settle it, and we would like to know.
trees.access: Free, open college campus green, self-guided visits welcome during daylight hours; occasionally closed off for commencement, Spoleto Festival performances or other campus events.
trees.transport: Downtown Charleston, walkable from the historic district; no dedicated transit stop needed
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for the yard rather than one tree: iron-fenced live oaks hung with Spanish moss, closed at the far end by the portico of Randolph Hall. Come in from George Street and stand at the sunken cistern.

trees.name: The Middleton Oak

location.address: Middleton Place, 4300 Ashley River Road, Charleston, SC 29414 (Sundial Garden)
location.neighbourhood: Middleton Place plantation gardens, Ashley River, near Summerville

trees.access: Paid entry (Middleton Place gardens, $28-32 adult admission, open daily 9am-5pm); stands in the Sundial Garden
trees.transport: Roughly 25-30 minutes by car northwest of downtown Charleston along Ashley River Road; no transit stop nearby
trees.story:
Until 2012 this oak was described as the largest tree in the eastern United States. It has also been losing large parts of its crown since 2008, which has cut into the volume of wood that made the claim. It is still standing and still alive.

The numbers from a 2004 measurement are still the ones people quote: a trunk 10.44 feet across, about ten metres round, a height of 67 feet and some 4,820 cubic feet of wood. It has been called the largest measured southern live oak. The Live Oak Society, whose members are the trees themselves, lists it as its First Vice President.

Charleston Magazine puts it at 900 to 1,000 years old. That is a figure repeated from one account to the next rather than measured, and it would make this oak several centuries older than the Angel Oak, so read it as a generous estimate rather than a date.

In 1997 a young oak propagated from it was planted just to the north, to help protect the old tree. That offspring is now about 26 feet tall, a reasonable start on the next thousand years.

The oak stands in the Sundial Garden at Middleton Place, about half an hour by car from downtown Charleston. Garden entry is paid.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a trunk about ten metres round under a crown thinned by losses since 2008, with a young oak raised from it standing just to the north. It stands in the Sundial Garden at Middleton Place.
